facts.statehood_note: Admitted 100 years after the Declaration of Independence, so it is called the Centennial State. Coloradans celebrate Colorado Day every August 1.
facts.nickname: The Centennial State (also called Colorful Colorado)
facts.motto: Nil sine numine (Latin: Nothing without Providence or Deity)
borders: Arizona (touches only at the Four Corners point)

symbols.name: White and lavender Rocky Mountain columbine (adopted 1899)
Stegosaurus (1982, after a fourth-grade class campaigned for two years)

facts.name_origin: From the Spanish word for "colored red." Congress chose the name for Colorado Territory in 1861.

government.chambers: Colorado Senate (35 members, 4-year terms) and Colorado House of Representatives (65 members, 2-year terms)
government.executive: Governor (4-year term; no more than two terms in a row). The constitution gives the governor "the supreme executive power of the state" and the job of making sure the laws are carried out. Other elected leaders include the lieutenant governor, secretary of state, state treasurer and attorney general.
government.courts: Colorado Supreme Court (7 justices who serve ten-year terms; the justices choose a chief justice who also leads the state court system). The state also has a Court of Appeals and 23 judicial districts.
government.local: 64 counties. Two of them, the City and County of Denver and the City and County of Broomfield, are a city and a county combined into one government.
government.constitution: Colorado's current and only constitution was drafted on March 14, 1876, approved by voters on July 1, 1876, and took effect at statehood on August 1, 1876. It has been amended many times since.
government.kid_line: "All political power is vested in and derived from the people." (Colorado Constitution, Article II, Section 1)

long_ago.nation: Ancestral Pueblo people (ancestors of today's Pueblo nations, including the Hopi)
long_ago.about: They came to the Mesa Verde area around 550 CE, farmed corn, beans and squash, and later built stone villages and cliff dwellings like Cliff Palace. By the end of the 1200s most had moved south to the Hopi mesas in Arizona and the Rio Grande pueblos in New Mexico.

The Ute are the oldest residents of Colorado; their own history says they lived here since the beginning of time. Ute bands such as the Mouache, Caputa and Weenuchiu lived in mountain valleys from the Front Range to the San Juan River, traveling well-known routes like the Ute Trail.
In the 1600s the Cheyenne moved west from the Great Lakes region to hunt across the High Plains. They traded buffalo robes at Bent's Fort on the Arkansas River in the 1830s and 1840s.
The Arapaho also moved onto the High Plains of Colorado and Wyoming in the 1600s and hunted buffalo there. Like the Cheyenne, they traded buffalo robes at Bent's Fort.
Apache and Comanche people lived in eastern and southeastern Colorado. Comanche and Kiowa traders also came to Bent's Fort.

today.about: A Ute nation with its own government, headquartered in Ignacio in southwest Colorado.
A Ute nation with its own government, headquartered in Towaoc in southwest Colorado.

first_peoples.today_note: The Southern Ute Indian Tribe and the Ute Mountain Ute Tribe are Colorado's two land-based tribes. The state's Commission of Indian Affairs also works with 46 other historic tribes of Colorado whose homelands included the state, and with Native people living in Colorado's cities.
sites: Mesa Verde National Park (Ancestral Pueblo cliff dwellings; the park protects the heritage of 26 tribes)
Sand Creek Massacre National Historic Site (Cheyenne and Arapaho history)
Bent's Old Fort National Historic Site (trading post where Cheyenne, Arapaho, Comanche, Kiowa, Hispanic and American traders met)

history.event: Indigenous Peoples are living in the land that is now Colorado. The Lindenmeier site holds tools about 10,700 years old.
Ancestral Pueblo people arrive in the Mesa Verde area, where they farm and later build pithouses and pueblos.
Ancestral Pueblo builders make most of Mesa Verde's cliff dwellings, like Cliff Palace. By about 1300, after long droughts and other hard times, the people have moved south to Arizona and New Mexico.
The Cheyenne and Arapaho move west from the Great Lakes region onto the High Plains. The Ute live in the mountains, and the Apache and Comanche in the east and southeast.
Spanish soldiers arrest U.S. Army explorer Zebulon Pike and his men in the San Luis Valley, land Spain claimed, and take them to Chihuahua.
William Bent and Ceran St. Vrain build an adobe trading fort on the Arkansas River. Cheyenne and Arapaho hunters trade buffalo robes there.

After the U.S.-Mexican War, Mexico gives up its northern lands in the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, including much of western and southern Colorado. The Ute homeland is now claimed by the United States.
Hispano families from the Taos area found San Luis, Colorado's first lasting town settled by newcomers, on April 9, 1851.
The gold rush brings thousands of newcomers to the Rocky Mountains to compete with the Ute, Cheyenne and Arapaho for land, water and game.
Congress creates Colorado Territory on February 28, 1861, just as the Civil War begins. Lawmakers leave out any words about slavery.
In the Civil War, the 1st Colorado Infantry fights for the Union at Glorieta Pass and other battles in New Mexico Territory.

On November 29, U.S. Army volunteers led by John Chivington attack a peaceful camp of about 750 Cheyenne and Arapaho people at Sand Creek and kill about 230, mostly women, children and elders. That same year the territorial legislature takes away Black men's right to vote.
After Congress forbids U.S. territories from denying men the vote because of race, Barney Ford returns to Denver and pushes for statehood with voting rights for all.
Voters approve the state constitution on July 1, and Colorado becomes the 38th state on August 1. At Casimiro Barela's urging, the constitution is published in English, Spanish and German.

trailblazers.name: Chipeta
trailblazers.text: Chipeta was the only woman of her time allowed on the Ute council. With her husband Ouray, a Tabeguache (Uncompahgre) Ute leader, she worked to keep peace with the United States and explained treaties to Ute women. In the end, the U.S. government still forced most Colorado Ute bands onto a reservation in Utah.

trailblazers.name: Clara Brown
trailblazers.text: Born enslaved in Virginia, she gained her freedom in Kentucky in the late 1850s and came west with a wagon train as a cook and midwife. In Central City she started the first laundry in Gilpin County, bought land and mines, and opened her home to people in need. She helped formerly enslaved people start new lives in Colorado and found her daughter Eliza Jane in 1882.

trailblazers.name: Barney Ford
trailblazers.group: Black American businessman and civil rights leader
trailblazers.text: Born enslaved in Virginia, he escaped to freedom in Chicago and came to Colorado in 1860. He built the People's Restaurant in Denver in 1863 and later hotels and businesses. When the territory took away Black men's right to vote in 1864 he fought back, pushed for Colorado statehood with voting rights for all, and is honored with a stained-glass window in the State Capitol.

trailblazers.name: Casimiro Barela
trailblazers.text: Born in Embudo, New Mexico, while it was still part of Mexico, he settled near Trinidad. In 1875 he was one of the delegates who wrote Colorado's constitution, and he urged that it be printed in Spanish, English and German. He served for many years in the state Senate and defended the rights of Spanish-speaking ranchers and other minority communities.

trailblazers.name: Chin Lin Sou
trailblazers.text: Born in southern China, he led Chinese railroad crews and came to Colorado to build the Denver Pacific line. From 1870 he supervised hundreds of Chinese miners near Black Hawk and Central City. When people falsely blamed Chinese miners for an 1874 fire in Central City, he stood up for them.

trailblazers.name: Justina Ford
trailblazers.text: In 1902 she became Denver's first licensed African American woman doctor. Hospitals would not let her work there, so she cared for families in their homes, serving Black, immigrant and poor white patients. Known as "the Baby Doctor," she delivered more than 7,000 babies in about 50 years.

landforms: Rocky Mountains (Mount Elbert, 14,440 feet, is the highest point in Colorado and in the Rocky Mountains)
Eastern Plains (part of the Great Plains)
San Luis Valley and the Great Sand Dunes
Colorado Plateau mesas and canyons (Mesa Verde)
Four Corners, the only place in the U.S. where four states meet
waters: Rio Grande (begins in the San Luis Valley)
geography.regions: About half of Colorado is the flat to rolling Eastern Plains; then come the Front Range, where most people live, the high Rocky Mountains and parks (wide mountain valleys), the San Luis Valley in the south-central part, and the Western Slope with mesas and canyons on the Colorado Plateau.

ecosystems.name: Alpine tundra
ecosystems.about: Above about 11,000 to 11,500 feet, it is too cold and windy for trees. Tiny cushion plants hug the ground to escape the wind, and some plants have fuzzy hairs or red coloring to stay warm.

ecosystems.name: Montane forest
ecosystems.about: The montane zone of the Rocky Mountains has the most kinds of plants and animals. Ponderosa pines grow on sunny slopes, can live more than 400 years, and their bark can smell like brown sugar on a warm day.

ecosystems.name: Plains grassland (prairie)
ecosystems.about: The Eastern Plains are mostly prairie, now largely farms and ranches. The state bird, the lark bunting, arrives on the plains in April and sings as it flies.

ecosystems.name: Sand dunes and wetlands of the San Luis Valley
ecosystems.about: Great Sand Dunes National Park has the tallest dunes in North America, next to grasslands, wetlands, forests and tundra. Elk are sometimes seen near the park road from fall through spring.

science.weather: Colorado is dry, and some part of the state is almost always in drought. Hail is the most common warm-season storm danger, and the Eastern Plains get some of the biggest hailstorms in North America; the plains are also at the western edge of Tornado Alley. Dry conditions make wildfires a serious danger, and in 2020 the state had its three largest wildfires on record.
science.resources: Colorado grew from gold and silver mining in the Colorado Mineral Belt. Today farms and ranches raise cattle, wheat, dairy, corn and hay, and mountain parks and snow bring many visitors.
science.highlight: Fossils! At Florissant Fossil Beds National Monument, volcanic ash and mudflows about 34 million years ago preserved petrified redwood stumps up to 14 feet wide and thousands of fossil insects and leaves. The state fossil, Stegosaurus, lived in Colorado about 150 million years ago.

g3_ss.title: Colorado's Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Find Denver on the map, learn what the governor and the General Assembly do, explore counties (including Denver's combined city and county), and read Article II, Section 1 of Colorado's constitution.

g3_ss.title: Colorado's First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Meet the Ancestral Pueblo people of Mesa Verde and the Ute, Cheyenne and Arapaho of long ago, then the Southern Ute and Ute Mountain Ute nations today.

g3_ss.title: Colorado Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Meet Chipeta, Clara Brown, Casimiro Barela and Justina Ford, and ask what new path each one opened.

g45_ss.title: Colorado's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: Compare Ancestral Pueblo farmers, mountain Ute bands and Plains Cheyenne and Arapaho, using Mesa Verde's cliff dwellings and Ute history as evidence.

g45_ss.title: Hispano Colorado, Bent's Fort and the Gold Rush
g45_ss.plan: Trace Spanish and Mexican claims, the 1848 treaty, San Luis (1851), trade at Bent's Fort and the 1858–1859 gold rush, and ask who gained and who lost land.

g45_ss.title: Colorado 1861–1876: Territory, War and Statehood
g45_ss.plan: Study Colorado Territory, the Civil War at Glorieta Pass, the Sand Creek Massacre, the fight over Black men's voting rights (Barney Ford), Chin Lin Sou and the 1876 constitution printed in three languages.

g3_sci.title: Life Above the Trees: Colorado's Alpine Tundra
g3_sci.plan: Find out why trees stop growing high on the mountains and how tiny tundra plants and animals survive cold and wind.

g3_sci.title: The Great Sand Dunes
g3_sci.plan: Learn how wind and water built North America's tallest dunes in the San Luis Valley, and meet the living things around them.

g3_sci.title: Hail, Snow and Sunshine: Colorado Weather
g3_sci.plan: Measure and chart weather, learn how hailstorms form on the plains, and how families get ready for storms and wildfire smoke.

g45_sci.title: Colorado Ecosystems from Plains to Peaks
g45_sci.plan: Compare prairie, montane forest and alpine tundra, and explain how elevation changes temperature and what can live there.

g45_sci.title: Drought, Wildfire and Colorado's Water
g45_sci.plan: Follow snowmelt from the Continental Divide into the Colorado, Rio Grande and Platte rivers, and use data to explain drought and wildfire risk.

g45_sci.title: Fossils of Colorado: Stegosaurus and Florissant
g45_sci.plan: Use the Florissant fossil beds and the state fossil, Stegosaurus, to explain how fossils form and what they tell us about ancient Colorado.
